quests.instruction: Choose the strongest opening for the proposal email.
quests.prompt: You lead a team and want to replace a 45-minute weekly status meeting with a written update. Your manager values team communication.
options: Many companies have replaced status meetings with written updates, so I think we should do the same as they have.
I have some thoughts about meetings that I would like to share with you at some point this month, if you have time.
I would like to propose trialling written weekly updates in place of our 45-minute status meeting, so that meeting time can go to solving problems.
The status meeting is a waste of everyone's time and should be scrapped immediately, before we lose any more hours.
quests.hint: The opening should state the proposal and connect it to a goal the manager shares.
quests.explanation: This opening states the change and links it to better use of time. The other choices insult the meeting, avoid a proposal or rely on what other firms do.

quests.instruction: Your manager worries that people will stop talking to each other. Choose the strongest reply.
quests.prompt: You are answering this concern in your proposal email.
options: If people stop talking, that will be their choice rather than a fault of the plan, and we cannot control that.
People talk plenty already, so this will not be an issue for the team, and the change will be easy to manage.
Written updates are the modern way to work, so people will adapt quickly, and I do not expect any difficulties.
That risk is real, so the trial would keep a fifteen-minute call for blockers; the time saved would go to the discussions that need it.
quests.hint: A strong reply admits what is fair and adds a specific safeguard.
quests.explanation: This reply concedes the risk and offers a concrete solution. The remaining options dismiss the concern or shift responsibility.

quests.instruction: Choose the most effective closing for the email.
quests.prompt: The email should end by inviting a decision.
options: A four-week trial would show whether written updates save time without hurting communication, and I can share the results with you at the end.
Please approve this proposal, because the current meetings are clearly not working for anyone on the team at all.
Written updates could be an option for the team, so please let me know whether you like the idea when you can.
I hope you will consider my proposal carefully and give me an answer as soon as you are able to do so.
quests.hint: A good closing proposes a small, measurable next step.
quests.explanation: The best closing suggests a limited trial and a way to judge it. The remaining options are vague or demanding.

quests.instruction: Choose the best thesis for the student council's proposal.
quests.prompt: The council wants to propose to the principal that students with free periods tutor younger pupils.
options: Students with free periods should be able to tutor younger pupils, because it deepens their own understanding and gives younger students extra help at no cost.
Peer tutoring is popular in many schools around the country and it should be introduced here, so that we do not fall behind.
Students are bored in free periods and deserve something better to do with the time that they are given each week.
Free periods are a waste of time for most students, and peer tutoring is the only sensible way to fix the problem.
quests.hint: The principal will care about learning benefits and cost.
quests.explanation: The best thesis gives two benefits that matter to a school. The alternatives rely on boredom, popularity or exaggeration.

quests.instruction: Choose the most convincing evidence for the proposal.
quests.prompt: The council needs evidence the principal will trust.
options: Many students said in a lunchtime survey that they would like to try tutoring, and several offered to help younger pupils.
Younger pupils enjoy working with older students and often ask for more help, according to a number of their teachers.
Tutoring is used by schools in several other countries around the world, and it has been growing in popularity for years.
In a term-long pilot in Year 9 maths, tutored pupils raised their average test score by six marks, and tutors said they felt more confident with the topics.
quests.hint: Strong evidence measures results.
quests.explanation: The pilot shows test-score gains and benefits to tutors. The other options show interest, popularity or preference.

quests.instruction: The principal worries that tutors might give incorrect explanations. Choose the best reply.
quests.prompt: The principal worries that tutors might explain topics incorrectly. Answer the concern without dismissing it.
options: Tutors could receive short training, and a teacher could check the sessions, keeping the benefits while reducing the risk.
Tutoring has worked elsewhere in the country, so mistakes are not a real concern for the school to worry about.
Students rarely make mistakes when they explain things to others, because explaining forces them to be careful.
Teachers make mistakes too, so this is not a special risk, and it should not be used as a reason to refuse.
quests.hint: The best reply offers a way to manage the risk.
quests.explanation: Training and checking address the concern directly. The others dismiss it or deflect.

quests.instruction: Choose the clearest position statement for a company memo.
quests.prompt: Managers want to allow staff to use an AI writing assistant for internal reports, but they are worried about errors.
options: AI tools are revolutionising the way that people work, and everyone in the company should embrace them as soon as possible.
The AI assistant will be used for internal reports from next month, and training sessions will be arranged for staff.
Staff may use the AI writing assistant to draft internal reports, provided a colleague checks every figure and claim before the report is shared.
Staff should be careful with the AI tool and use their own judgement whenever they decide to include what it writes.
quests.hint: A policy statement says what is allowed and under what condition.
quests.explanation: This statement sets a rule and a condition. The rest are slogans, vague advice or a plain announcement.

quests.instruction: What is the main weakness in this argument?
quests.prompt: 'Other firms use the AI tool and have not had problems, so ours will be fine.'
options: It attacks the people who oppose the tool, rather than answering their concerns about accuracy.
It relies on emotion instead of facts, and it tries to make the reader afraid of the tool.
It presents only two options and ignores the possibility that a middle course might be better.
It assumes other firms' experience predicts ours without evidence.
quests.hint: Ask what must be true for the conclusion to follow.
quests.explanation: The argument assumes that other firms' results transfer to ours. There is no personal attack, false choice or emotional appeal.

quests.instruction: Choose the best revision.
quests.prompt: Original: 'The AI tool is always accurate, so checking is a waste of time.'
options: The AI tool is accurate enough that only major reports need checking, because small reports carry little risk.
The AI tool is nearly always accurate, so checking is rarely necessary and would only slow down the team.
The AI tool is often accurate, but it can make confident mistakes, so a quick check is still worth the time.
The AI tool is usually right, but checking is optional for busy staff who have to meet several deadlines.
quests.hint: Replace the overgeneralisation with a fair claim and a reason.
quests.explanation: The right revision limits the claim and explains why checking is worthwhile. The others still weaken the case for checking.

quests.instruction: Choose the best public reply.
quests.prompt: A customer's review reads: 'Waited 40 minutes for my order and nobody apologised.' You manage the café.
options: We serve hundreds of happy customers every week, so this review is not typical of the service that we normally provide.
We are sorry about the wait and that no one apologised; that is not the service we want to give. Please contact us so we can put it right.
We are sorry to hear about the wait, but our records show a very busy Saturday, so some delays were unavoidable that day.
We are sorry you feel that way about your visit, and we hope that you will give us another try in the near future.
quests.hint: A good reply acknowledges the complaint, does not make excuses and offers a next step.
quests.explanation: This reply accepts responsibility and offers to fix the problem. The others make excuses, offer a non-apology or dismiss the review.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest reason for replying to every negative review.
quests.prompt: The business owner is deciding on a policy.
options: Negative reviews upset staff, so a reply from the manager can make the team feel supported and less discouraged.
Replying shows the business is in charge of its reputation, and it lets the owner correct anything that is inaccurate.
Future customers read the replies as well as the reviews, so a helpful response shows how the business treats problems.
Other businesses in the area reply to every review they receive, so a business that stays silent may look out of step.
quests.hint: Focus on the reader of the replies.
quests.explanation: The best reason identifies who benefits and how. The other choices focus on staff feelings, imitation or image.

quests.instruction: A colleague says replying publicly draws more attention to complaints. Choose the response that concedes fairly and answers.
quests.prompt: Respond in a meeting.
options: Complaints get attention anyway, so we should reply to every one of them in full detail and explain exactly what went wrong.
That is not true, because customers rarely notice complaints unless the business draws attention to them by replying at length.
Attention is inevitable whatever we do, so replying is pointless and the team should spend its time on service instead.
That can happen, so replies should be short and calm and move detailed talks to private messages; the goal is to show good handling, not to argue.
quests.hint: The best response accepts part of the concern and adapts the plan.
quests.explanation: The best response concedes the risk and sets guidelines. The others deny, give up or overreact.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest thesis for a letter to the rail company.
quests.prompt: You want a quiet carriage on morning commuter trains.
options: Quiet carriages are already used by other rail companies with success, so this one should offer them on its own trains.
Commuter trains should keep one carriage quiet during morning peak hours, so that passengers who need calm can work or rest without others' calls and music.
Some passengers find trains noisy at busy times, which is a problem that the rail company should take seriously and study.
Commuters deserve peace and quiet on the way to work, and the rail company should listen to what its passengers want.
quests.hint: The thesis should be specific about what, when and why.
quests.explanation: The best thesis names the change, the time and the benefit. The rest are general, rely on imitation or only describe.

quests.instruction: Which objection is most serious and should be answered in the letter?
quests.prompt: Think about the effect on other passengers.
options: Some passengers might prefer to talk on the phone during their journey, especially when they are travelling for work.
Trains have carriages of different lengths and layouts, so the quiet area might not be the same size on every train.
Peak trains are crowded, so reserving a carriage could push more passengers into the others.
Quiet carriages have not been tested on every line, so the results from one route may not apply to another.
quests.hint: A serious objection points to a real cost for many people.
quests.explanation: Crowding affects all passengers and threatens the plan's fairness. The other objections are minor or about preference.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest reply to the crowding objection.
quests.prompt: Answer the concern that a quiet carriage will make peak trains more crowded.
options: Crowding already exists at peak times, so a quiet carriage will make no real difference to how full the trains are.
Passengers who want quiet should travel at other times, when the trains are emptier and the noise is much lower.
The quiet carriage could be an ordinary carriage open to everyone who follows the rule, so total capacity is not reduced.
Crowding will be a problem whatever the railway does, so there is little point in changing one carriage on a train.
quests.hint: Show that the concern can be solved.
quests.explanation: The best reply explains that seats stay available to all. The remaining options dismiss or shift the problem.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest evidence for installing motion-sensor lights.
quests.prompt: A facilities manager wants proof before spending money.
options: Motion-sensor lights are becoming more common in modern offices, and many new buildings are now fitted with them.
In the pilot on floor 3, lights were on for 40% fewer hours over two months, cutting that floor's electricity bill by £210.
Several staff said they like the idea of automatic lights, and a few said they would be glad not to touch the switches.
Lights use electricity, which costs money for the company, and the bill rises each year as prices go up.
quests.hint: Look for measured results in a real setting.
quests.explanation: The pilot shows a measured reduction and a cost. The rest are general trends or opinions.

quests.instruction: Choose the sentence that best explains why the evidence supports the claim.
quests.prompt: Evidence: lights on for 40% fewer hours after sensors were fitted.
options: Sensors can be bought from many different suppliers, and the price of a basic unit has fallen in recent years.
Forty percent is a large number of hours over two months, and it shows that the lights were on far too often.
Lights that are switched off use no electricity at all, so any system that switches them off will save some money.
Because much of the floor's lighting had been on in empty rooms, sensors remove waste without changing how staff work.
quests.hint: Explain why the change in hours matters.
quests.explanation: The right sentence links fewer hours to reduced waste. The alternatives repeat, describe or state the obvious.

quests.instruction: Choose the best final recommendation.
quests.prompt: You are writing to the facilities manager.
options: Sensors seem good, and maybe the company could think about extending them to other floors when there is time to do so.
It would be sensible to consider the sensors, among other options, at some point in the coming year or so.
I recommend extending the sensors to the remaining floors in stages, starting with the two that are empty most evenings, and reviewing the savings after three months.
The sensors have worked on one floor, so they should be installed everywhere in the building immediately, without delay.
quests.hint: A good recommendation is specific and measured.
quests.explanation: The correct recommendation gives a plan and a review. The remaining options rush, hesitate or stay vague.

quests.instruction: Choose the most balanced and clear position.
quests.prompt: The council is consulting residents about turning the Baker Street car park into a market square.
options: The council should convert the car park because markets are better than parked cars, and the town needs more places to meet.
The council should convert the Baker Street car park into a market square, provided that disabled parking bays and a nearby alternative car park are kept.
There are strong arguments for and against turning the car park into a market square, and the council should weigh them all.
The car park should be kept as it is, because drivers need somewhere to park and shoppers would be put off by any change.
quests.hint: A balanced position takes a stand and names a condition.
quests.explanation: The best position supports the plan and protects a key need. The other choices are one-sided or avoid a position.

quests.instruction: Which evidence best supports the claim that the car park is underused?
quests.prompt: The council needs to know whether the car park is really underused. Which evidence answers that most directly?
options: Parking is expensive in the town centre, and many drivers complain about the price of a two-hour stay.
On the last four Saturdays, fewer than half of its 120 spaces were taken by 2 p.m.
The car park is in the middle of the town centre, next to the bus station and two of the main shops.
The market on Elm Street draws large crowds each week, and its stallholders say trade has grown steadily.
quests.hint: Evidence about use must show how many spaces are filled.
quests.explanation: Counts of spaces taken are direct evidence. The others describe location, another market or cost.

quests.instruction: Choose the best sentence for a consultation leaflet aimed at local shopkeepers.
quests.prompt: Shopkeepers worry about losing customers who drive.
options: The plan will go ahead whatever shopkeepers say, so it is better for them to adapt early and make the most of the new market.
Shopkeepers who object simply fear change, but once the market opens they will be glad that the council went ahead with the plan.
We understand that customers who drive matter to your business, so the plan keeps a short walk to the nearest car park and adds a weekly market that may bring extra visitors.
A market square is a modern idea that everyone will love, and shopkeepers will soon see that the change is good for them, whatever they may fear.
quests.hint: Acknowledge the reader's concern and offer a reason to support the plan.
quests.explanation: This sentence respects the concern and provides a benefit. The alternatives dismiss, threaten or overpromise.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest claim with a reason.
quests.prompt: A university is considering anonymous marking for coursework.
options: Universities should mark anonymously because most universities now do, and it would look odd for ours to be different.
Coursework marking is important, and anonymity may help in some cases, though it may not be needed in every course.
Coursework should be marked anonymously, because it reduces the chance that a marker's impressions of a student affect the grade.
Anonymous marking is fairer than named marking, which is not fair to students who are marked down by their reputation.
quests.hint: The reason should explain how anonymity leads to fairness.
quests.explanation: The best answer explains how the change reduces bias. The other choices repeat, rely on popularity or hedge.

quests.instruction: What assumption does this argument make?
quests.prompt: 'Anonymous marking removes bias, so all grades will be fair.'
options: It assumes students prefer named marking, because they can then ask the marker for personal advice.
It assumes fair grades do not matter as much as the speed at which coursework is returned to students.
It assumes anonymous marking is expensive to run, so universities must be saving money by using it.
It assumes bias about a student's identity is the only cause of unfairness.
quests.hint: What must be true for 'all grades will be fair' to follow?
quests.explanation: The argument treats identity bias as the only source of unfairness. Marking can also be unfair for other reasons, such as unclear criteria.

quests.instruction: Choose the best revision.
quests.prompt: Original: 'Anonymous marking is perfect. Nobody could disagree with it.'
options: Anonymous marking is not a complete solution, but it removes one source of bias that students cannot control; clear mark schemes would address others.
Anonymous marking should be used in every course, though a few other opinions exist and should be listened to politely.
Anonymous marking is nearly perfect, and only a few people who do not understand it could disagree with the idea.
Anonymous marking removes bias from grading and fixes unfairness, so students can be confident that every grade is right.
quests.hint: Replace overstatement with a fair claim and a complementary step.
quests.explanation: This revision accepts limits and adds a reasonable next step. The remaining options still overstate or avoid detail.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest evidence for repairing rather than replacing a phone.
quests.prompt: You are writing a consumer advice column.
options: A £90 battery replacement gave my three-year-old phone another two years of use, compared with £650 for a new model.
New phones are expensive, and many people struggle to afford them, so repairs have to be the more sensible choice.
Everybody I know keeps their phone for several years, and most of them say they would repair it rather than replace it.
Repairing phones is generally more environmentally friendly than replacing them, and it keeps materials in use for longer.
quests.hint: Strong evidence gives actual costs and results.
quests.explanation: This answer gives specific costs and outcome. The other choices state opinions or general claims.

quests.instruction: Which comparison is fair?
quests.prompt: Claim: Repairing a phone is cheaper than replacing it.
options: The cost of a repair compared with a friend's discount on a new phone, taken from a single offer in the shops.
The cost of one screen repair compared with the cost of a phone accessory, such as a case or a charger, over a year.
The price of a repair compared with the launch price of the newest premium model, on the day that it goes on sale.
The total cost of repairing a phone over two years compared with the total cost of buying a new one for the same period.
quests.hint: A fair comparison uses the same time period and equivalent options.
quests.explanation: The right comparison matches costs over the same period. The remaining options compare unequal items.

quests.instruction: A friend says repairs can fail and new phones come with warranties. Choose the best reply.
quests.prompt: Concede fairly and answer.
options: Many people repair phones every year, so failures must be rare, and it is not worth worrying about a warranty.
Warranties matter a great deal, so it is better to buy a new phone every time and avoid repairs altogether.
That is fair, so choose a repairer that guarantees its work; a repair with a warranty still costs far less than a new phone.
Repairs never fail, so warranties are irrelevant, and it is much smarter to spend a little money on a good repair.
quests.hint: Accept the valid part, then answer it with a specific solution.
quests.explanation: This reply concedes the risk and suggests a guarantee. The other choices deny, give up or use popularity.

quests.instruction: Choose the strongest claim.
quests.prompt: A company offers a workplace wellness scheme that shares individual fitness tracker data with employers.
options: Fitness tracker data is private, and no company should ever be allowed to look at it, whatever the reason for asking.
Fitness trackers are popular with many staff, and companies want to use the data to help people stay healthy and active.
Employers who collect fitness data clearly want to control their staff, and any scheme of this kind should be stopped.
Employers should not receive individual fitness tracker data, because staff cannot freely choose to share information that might influence how they are seen at work.
quests.hint: A strong claim explains why the practice is a problem.
quests.explanation: This claim gives a specific reason based on freedom of choice. The others exaggerate, accuse or describe.

quests.instruction: A manager says the scheme is voluntary, so it is fair. What is missing from the argument?
quests.prompt: Identify the gap.
options: Evidence that staff can decline without any pressure or disadvantage.
Evidence that regular exercise is healthy for most people.
A list of the tracker brands staff can choose from.
Evidence that fitness trackers are popular among employees.
quests.hint: Ask what 'voluntary' depends on.
quests.explanation: 'Voluntary' only makes the scheme fair if declining carries no penalty. The other pieces do not address that.

quests.instruction: Choose the best compromise proposal.
quests.prompt: The company wants to encourage healthy habits while respecting privacy.
options: Offer a scheme where individual data is shared only with senior managers, who are trained to keep it strictly confidential.
Offer a wellness scheme that uses anonymous, group-level results, so the company can see overall participation without seeing any individual's data.
Keep the scheme as it is and tell staff that privacy concerns are not a problem, because the data is stored securely.
Offer the scheme to everyone and record who declines, so that managers can follow up with those who did not take part.
quests.hint: A good compromise meets both goals.
quests.explanation: This proposal protects privacy while achieving the company's aim. The others keep the privacy risk.
